official.description: The Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship Programme is a New Zealand Government scholarship administered by Education New Zealand | Manapou ki te Ao. Full scholarships for scholars studying in New Zealand pay full tuition fees plus a living allowance, an establishment allowance, medical insurance, tutoring support, travel to and from the scholar's country, travel insurance, travel-home trips for scholars studying over 1.6 years, a reintegration allowance on return, and help with research and thesis costs for many postgraduate students. Awards are conditional on a two-year post-scholarship contribution to the scholar's own country and on having lived in that country for the two years before applying.
purpose: Manaaki New Zealand Scholarships help build prosperity, security, and sustainable growth in partner countries and fosters a lifetime connection to Aotearoa New Zealand and the leaders of tomorrow.

Recipients of a Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship build life-long connections to each other and to Aotearoa New Zealand while gaining a globally recognised education, an authentically New Zealand experience, and the tools to help their countries achieve the futures they deserve.

The Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship Programme aims to enhance the mana of partner countries and Aotearoa New Zealand through manaakitanga - the act of hosting, supporting and honouring manaaki scholars.
"The purpose of a Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship is to invest in the education of citizens from developing countries, enabling them to positively impact their communities and country's development."

Scholars must contribute to their country's development: "We expect scholars to contribute to their country's social or economic development for at least two years after completing their scholarship study and this is a condition of the scholarship."
study_type: Undergraduate and postgraduate (tertiary) study in New Zealand, or at a Pacific university
"Scholars can study abroad in New Zealand at one of eight universities or three institutes of technology."

Pacific study option: eligible citizens from Kiribati, Niue, Samoa, Solomon Islands, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu can apply to study at one of two Pacific universities (University of the South Pacific or Fiji National University).
The programme also runs separate strands: Thematic Short Term Training Scholarships, Vocational Short Term Training Scholarships, and English Language Training for Officials Scholarships.
official.degree_award: Full tertiary qualification at a New Zealand university or institute of technology, or at a Pacific university. The scholarship funds the programme of study, not a standalone short-term award.
official.duration: "You must complete your study within the time period allocated by your education institution for your chosen academic programme." The published duration is therefore set by the institution and programme rather than a single Manaaki figure. Scholars studying over 1.6 years are entitled to travel home to visit family, which is the only published duration-derived entitlement.
official.application_cycle: Annual. "Tertiary applications for the Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship Programme have now closed." A separate Samoa Foundation intake opens midnight 4 August 2026 and closes midday 4 September 2026. The programme applies early-closure pressure: "the Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship Programme application system may close early to countries with a large volume of applications. To avoid disappointment, we strongly recommend applying as early as possible."
official.deadline_central_display: Tertiary applications for the Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship Programme have now closed. The Samoa Foundation intake opens midnight 4 August 2026 and closes midday 4 September 2026. No date is published for the next general tertiary round, and applications may close early for countries with a large volume of applications, so Education New Zealand strongly recommends applying as early as possible.
official.deadline_note: No central closing date is published for the general tertiary round, which is stated only as closed. The only published dates in the cycle are the Samoa Foundation window (midnight 4 August 2026 to midday 4 September 2026). Deadlines also vary by pathway: Pacific scholars applying to study in the Pacific, Cook Islands scholars applying to their own Government scholarships, and country-level application routes each run on their own schedule.
official.funding_label: "With a full Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship, scholars studying in New Zealand receive: Full tuition fees. Living allowance. This will help with basic living expenses. If you commence your scholarship study programme in your home country, your stipend will be adjusted to reflect the difference in living costs around the world. And establishment allowance to help with set-up costs in New Zealand. For example, you can use it for accommodation expenses, textbooks, or other study materials. Medical insurance when you are in your New Zealand. Tutoring costs to assist with additional academic support if needed. Travel to and from your own country. This is for travel from your own country at the start of the scholarship, and for return travel at the end of your scholarship. Travel insurance. Travel home during your scholarship. Scholars studying over 1.6 years are entitled to travel home to visit family. We usually allow for one or two trips, depending on the length. Reintegration allowance. This is to help with set-up costs upon your return to your home country. Help with research and thesis costs for many postgraduate students." No dollar figures are published on the pages read.
official.funding_period: The period of the academic programme allocated by the scholar's education institution; the scholar must complete their study within that time. No fixed number of years is published on the pages read.
official.tuition_coverage: "Full tuition fees" are covered for scholars studying in New Zealand under a full Manaaki New Zealand Scholarship. Tuition is paid through the scholarship rather than waived at application stage, and the scholarship offer is what authorises the institution to accept the scholar.
official.living_cost_coverage: "Living allowance. This will help with basic living expenses. If you commence your scholarship study programme in your home country, your stipend will be adjusted to reflect the difference in living costs around the world." Plus an establishment allowance "to help with set-up costs in New Zealand. For example, you can use it for accommodation expenses, textbooks, or other study materials"; medical insurance while in New Zealand; tutoring costs for additional academic support if needed; a reintegration allowance for set-up costs on return home; and help with research and thesis costs for many postgraduate students.
official.travel_coverage: "Travel to and from your own country. This is for travel from your own country at the start of the scholarship, and for return travel at the end of your scholarship." Plus "Travel insurance." And "Travel home during your scholarship. Scholars studying over 1.6 years are entitled to travel home to visit family. We usually allow for one or two trips, depending on the length." Your education institution's International Students Office organises the travel to your study location.
official.tuition_rule: "Full tuition fees." Tuition is included in the scholarship and is not itemised as a separate cap. Note that the scholar is responsible for organising their own accommodation: "Please note you will be responsible for organising accommodation at your study location." The establishment allowance is, however, explicitly usable for accommodation expenses.

Applicants in the final year of high school when they apply, or applying in the academic year immediately after completing high school, are not required to have work experience.
Only subjects eligible for the applicant's country are funded.
masters: Available for postgraduate study in New Zealand.
Postgraduate applicants must have relevant work experience: one year of full-time (30+ hours per week) or two years of part-time (up to 29 hours per week), paid, unpaid or voluntary.

Preference in selection is given to applicants who demonstrate how their proposed course aligns to their current work experience, and to applicants who will continue working in their current job sector after the scholarship.
Many postgraduate students receive help with research and thesis costs.

General English guide for postgraduate study is an overall IELTS 6.5 with no band less than 6.0, TOEFL iBT 90 with a writing score of 21, PTE Academic 58 with no communicative skills score below 50, or Cambridge Academic English (advanced) 176 with no band below 169. Each institution sets its own minimum and some courses require higher.
phd: PhD applicants should identify and contact suitable PhD supervisors at New Zealand universities as early as possible.

"PhD scholarship applicants who make it to the interview stage will need to provide evidence at the interview that they have either secured a supervisor or are in active discussions with a potential supervisor."

official.selection_notes: "Award recipients are selected through a global, annual, and competitive application process." Applications may close early for countries with a large volume of applications. Education New Zealand publishes no assessment weighting, panel composition, score-based ranking or notification date on the pages read, and states that how long the process takes depends on the number of applicants received for a country.

Must maintain an acceptable standard of conduct as specified in the Scholarship Conditions in the Letter of Scholarship Offer, from the date of departure from their home country until the date they return upon completion of the scholarship. Acceptable conduct includes abiding by the laws of the study country, treating others with respect, behaving with honesty and integrity, and acting in a manner that reflects the scholar's role as a representative of their home country.
Must read and follow the relevant Operational Policy Handbook â€” the NZ Scholar version for study in New Zealand, or the Pacific Scholar version for study in the Pacific.

Must meet any pre-requisite conditions stated in the Scholarship Letter of Offer, such as obtaining a valid student visa before leaving their home country or completing further English language training; otherwise "the scholarship offer will be withdrawn".

application_readiness_checklist: Confirm your citizenship is on the eligible list â€” this is the first gate and the programme says scholarships are only available to citizens of eligible regions and countries.

Confirm you have lived in your home country for the two years before applying, unless you have been on a diplomatic assignment for your home country (dependants included) or have been studying overseas.
Postgraduate applicants: evidence one year of full-time (30+ hours per week) or two years of part-time (up to 29 hours per week) relevant work experience. Paid, unpaid or voluntary all count.
Age: you must be 18 at signing the scholarship letter of offer; 17 at commencement is allowed for the Samoa Foundation intake.
Check that the subject you want to study is eligible for your country â€” scholarships are only available for specific subjects.
Pick your institution and courses and check their minimum academic and English entry requirements. You do not apply for admission yet, but you must be likely to qualify.
PhD applicants: contact and identify potential supervisors now. At interview you must evidence a secured supervisor or active discussions.
Have your academic transcript for the qualification ready, including the Grading Scale â€” you must upload it with the application (not required for Samoa Foundation).
Be ready with verified English-translated transcripts and completion certificates if shortlisted.
If you are not from a country where the programme organises and pays for your IELTS, book an approved English test early â€” testing takes weeks and you must have passed it within the last 12 months.
If sitting IELTS, have a valid passport and a digital colour copy ready.
Keep receipts for visa and medical costs you pay up front; your institution reimburses them after you arrive.
Plan to attend a pre-departure briefing from the New Zealand Embassy or High Commission, or download it.
Understand you must return home and contribute to your country's social or economic development for at least two years afterwards. This is a condition, not a hope.
Read the Operational Policy Handbook and the Scholarship Conditions before you sign the offer, because the offer may carry pre-requisite conditions that can withdraw it.
important_advice_for_students: This is one of the most complete government scholarships available: full tuition fees, living allowance, establishment allowance, medical insurance, travel both ways, travel insurance, travel home, reintegration allowance and research/thesis help. The main thing it does not do is find you a room â€” you organise your own accommodation, though the establishment allowance can be spent on it.

Do not delay. Education New Zealand states the application system may close early for countries with a large volume of applications and strongly recommends applying as early as possible. An early application matters more here than in most schemes.

The two-year home-country contribution is a condition of the scholarship, not a suggestion. You must contribute to your country's social or economic development for at least two years after finishing. If you want to emigrate permanently straight after, this scheme is a poor fit.
Work experience is the gate most postgraduate applicants trip on. One year of full-time or two years of part-time, and it can be unpaid or voluntary, so community work counts if it is relevant.

You do not need an English test score at application. Testing happens in the final selection stages and only shortlisted applicants need it. If you are from a listed Pacific or Asian country the programme books and pays for your IELTS; if you are not, you pay and get reimbursed by your institution on arrival.
Bring the Grading Scale with your transcript. Uploading the transcript without it is a published requirement failure.

One published list item appears internally inconsistent. The Manaaki eligibility page says work experience is not required for applicants "in paid or unpaid employment", which reads as a typo for applicants not in employment. If your case is ambiguous, ask Education New Zealand rather than assuming.

Visa timing is a real risk. You only apply for a student visa after you are offered and accept, the process takes two to three months and includes medical tests, and if you do not get a visa your scholarship is withdrawn. Have money ready for the upfront costs.
Know which costs are not reimbursed: travel to the medical check and to the visa interview, police clearance fee, courier fee, passport application and renewal fees, and dependent visa fees.

If your English is just below the entry requirement, ask whether you are eligible for funded English language training. It can be up to a year in New Zealand for Pacific and Timor-Leste applicants, up to a year in your home country for Cambodia, Lao PDR and Indonesia, and up to a semester in New Zealand otherwise. It is not available for PhD applicants.

Previous Manaaki recipients: check your stand-down. Two years after a completed tertiary scholarship, five years after an academic termination or a return home without completing a qualification, two years after certain personal-termination cases, and permanently if you were terminated for inappropriate conduct.

The academic conditions are strict and enforced by termination. You must attend classes, complete compulsory assignments, sit all exams and meet all course requirements on time, and you must complete within the period your institution allocates.
Conduct obligations start the day you leave home and run until you return. They include behaving as a representative of your home country, and New Zealand's family-violence laws apply in full.
common_rejection_risks: Citizenship outside the eligible regions and countries.
Not having resided in your home country for the two years before applying, with no qualifying exception.
Postgraduate applicants without one year of full-time or two years of part-time relevant work experience.
Applying for a subject that is not eligible for your country.
Being likely to fall short of the institution's academic or English entry requirements.
Uploading an academic transcript without the Grading Scale.
Being 17 at signing of the scholarship letter of offer outside the Samoa Foundation intake.
Missing the deadline, or losing the race in a country where the portal closes early for high application volumes.
Being within a stand-down period, or barred under the five-year, two-year or permanent-prohibition alumni rules.
Failing to provide verified English-translated transcripts and completion certificates after shortlisting.
PhD applicants reaching interview without a secured supervisor or evidence of active discussions.
Not obtaining a student visa within the required time, which withdraws the scholarship.
Failing to meet pre-requisite conditions in the Scholarship Letter of Offer, which withdraws the offer.
Failing to meet the academic conditions, which terminates the scholarship.
Applying as a Cook Islands citizen to Manaaki rather than to the Cook Islands Government scholarships.
Failing to book an English test promptly after shortlisting, since testing takes several weeks.
estimated_uncovered_costs: Accommodation, which you must organise yourself, though the establishment allowance is explicitly usable for accommodation expenses.
Travel to the location where your immigration medical check occurs â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Travel to the location where your visa interview occurs â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Police clearance fee â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Courier fee for the visa application â€” explicitly not reimbursed.
Passport application fee and passport renewal fee â€” explicitly not reimbursed.

English language testing costs for shortlisted applicants outside the programme's IELTS list, before reimbursement by your institution on arrival.

Anything not covered by the published list of benefits, including costs arising if your programme length exceeds the time your institution allocated, since the scholarship is terminated for missing the academic conditions.
The cost of any prior scholarship debt or the consequences of not completing the two-year post-scholarship contribution to your own country.

Payment receipts for the visa application fee, immigration levy and one immigration medical check fee â€” required to claim reimbursement from your education institution.

Do not keep receipts for anything else expecting reimbursement: travel to the medical check, travel to the visa interview, police clearance, courier, passport fees and dependent visa fees are all published as not reimbursed.

Selection preferences to evidence in the application: how your proposed course aligns to your current work experience, that you will continue in your current job sector, and how you will contribute to your country's social and economic development after the scholarship.

Early-closure rule and advice: the application system may close early for countries with a large volume of applications, and applicants are strongly recommended to apply as early as possible

Full financial package published for scholars studying in New Zealand: full tuition fees; living allowance (adjusted if the programme commences in the home country); establishment allowance for set-up costs usable for accommodation, textbooks and other study materials; medical insurance in New Zealand; tutoring costs for additional academic support; travel to and from the scholar's own country at the start and end; travel insurance; travel home during the scholarship for scholars studying over 1.6 years; reintegration allowance for return set-up costs; and help with research and thesis costs for many postgraduate students
Accommodation: the scholar is responsible for organising accommodation at the study location
Travel and arrival: the education institution's International Students Office organises travel to the study location and looks after the scholar on arrival
Age: 18 at signing the scholarship letter of offer; Samoa Foundation applicants may be 17 at commencement; no upper age limit but preference for applicants under 40

Work experience for postgraduates: one year of full-time (30+ hours per week) or two years of part-time (up to 29 hours per week), paid, unpaid or voluntary; not required for final-year-of-high-school applicants, applicants in the academic year immediately after completing high school, and â€” as the page states â€” applicants in paid or unpaid employment

Selection preferences: alignment of the proposed course with current work experience; continuing in the current job sector after the scholarship; clear description of contribution to the country's social and economic development afterwards

Two-year home-country contribution: scholars are expected to contribute to their country's social or economic development for at least two years after completing their scholarship study, and this is a condition of the scholarship

Residency requirement: two years of residence in the home country prior to applying, with exceptions for diplomatic assignment for the home country (including dependants) and for applicants enrolled in a course of study overseas

Academic and English requirements are set by the preferred education institution; general guide for postgraduate is IELTS 6.5 (no band below 6.0), TOEFL iBT 90 (writing 21), PTE Academic 58 (no skill below 50), Cambridge Academic English advanced 176 (no band below 169); for undergraduate IELTS 6.0 (no band below 5.5), TOEFL iBT 80 (writing 21), PTE 50 (no skill below 42), Cambridge 169 (no band below 162)
English testing only at shortlist stage, not at application, and not for candidates applying for tertiary study in the Pacific

IELTS organised and paid by the programme for shortlisted applicants from Cambodia, Indonesia, Fiji, French Pacific (New Caledonia, French Polynesia, Wallis and Futuna), Kiribati, Lao PDR, Naoero, North Pacific (Federated States of Micronesia, Palau, Marshall Islands), Papua New Guinea, Samoa (except Samoa Foundation applicants), Solomon Islands, Timor-Leste, Tonga, Tuvalu and Vanuatu; all other shortlisted applicants pay their own and are reimbursed by their tertiary institution on arrival
IELTS documentation rule: all IELTS applicants need a valid passport and all IELTS applications must include a digital colour copy of the passport

English language training may be funded for some preferred candidates: up to one year in New Zealand for Pacific and Timor-Leste applicants; up to one year in their home country for Cambodia, Lao PDR and Indonesia; up to one semester in New Zealand for all other eligible countries; not available for PhD applicants

Alumni and stand-down rules: two-year stand-down after a completed tertiary scholarship; five-year bar after academic termination, academic downgrade, or returning home without completing a qualification; two-year bar after voluntary withdrawal for unforeseen personal circumstances or personal-grounds downgrade; permanent prohibition after termination for inappropriate conduct; stand-down also applies after an ELTO or Short-Term Training Scholarship

Visa rule: apply for a student visa only after being offered and accepting; the process takes two to three months and involves medical tests; a recipient who does not get a student visa has the scholarship withdrawn; only those who qualify for a student visa can take up the scholarship
Reimbursed costs on production of receipts: visa application fee and immigration levy; immigration medical check fee (maximum of one)

Non-reimbursed costs: travel to the medical check location, travel to the visa interview location, police clearance fee, courier fee for the visa application, passport application fee, passport renewal fee, and dependent's visa fees

Application documents: academic transcript for the qualification including the Grading Scale is required at application and is not required for Samoa Foundation applicants; shortlisted applicants provide verified English-translated copies of academic transcripts and completion certificates
PhD rule: applicants should identify and contact supervisors early, and those reaching interview must evidence a secured supervisor or active discussions
Do not apply for institutional admission until notified as a preferred candidate

Academic conditions: must complete study within the time allocated by the education institution; must attend classes, complete compulsory assignment and sit all exams; must meet all course requirements on time; failure terminates the scholarship

Conduct requirements apply from departure from the home country until return on completion: obey the laws of the study country, treat others with respect, behave with honesty and integrity, and act as a representative of the home country; family violence and child abuse are offences
Institutions must follow the Education (Pastoral Care of Tertiary and International Learners) Code of Practice 2021
Pre-requisite conditions may apply and failure withdraws the offer; examples given are a valid student visa before leaving the home country and completing more English language training

official.description: The University of Otago Global Scholarship is an Otago Entrance Scholarship for new international undergraduate students from a nominated list of 13 countries and territories. It is worth NZD $15,000 with a one-year tenure and is paid only as a credit towards tuition fees. There is no separate scholarship application: offshore applicants are assessed automatically during the admission process by agreeing in their eVision application for study to be considered for international scholarships, and the offer must be actively accepted by the deadline in the scholarship offer letter in addition to accepting the admission offer.

"The University of Otago | Otaku Whakaihu Waka Global Scholarships are University of Otago | Otaku Whakaihu Waka Entrance Scholarships and are subject to the standard Undergraduate Entrance Scholarship terms and conditions, except for the following conditions which supersede the normal Entrance Scholarship terms and conditions as indicated."

On the international scholarships index, the University states the Global Scholarship is for "new international Bachelor degree students commencing full-time undergraduate study" holding one of thirteen listed passports, with unlimited offers.

official.duration: "The value of the scholarship is $15,000 with a one-year tenure." The scholarship is formally awarded once, and its entitlement is cancelled if the student's enrolment is terminated, or the student withdraws or stops study.

important_advice_for_students: This is tuition money only. $15,000 goes to your fees and nothing else. There is no living allowance, no accommodation, no airfare. Plan your living costs separately.

There is no scholarship application. The single most important administrative step is ticking the box in your eVision admission application that agrees to being considered for international scholarships. Miss it and you are not in the pool.

Accepting admission and accepting the scholarship are two separate actions with two separate deadlines. The scholarship offer must be actively accepted by the deadline in the scholarship offer letter, in addition to accepting the admission offer.

Deferral is not allowed. The Global Scholarship expressly overrides the normal entrance-scholarship condition to say deferral is not possible, so do not defer your start expecting to keep it.

You cannot stack it with another Otago Entrance Scholarship. Unless an exception applies, holding both is not permitted, and if you are awarded another UES you will normally get the highest-value one.
If your country's government sponsors you, you are ineligible. This is aimed at self-funding or privately funded international students.

Government sponsorship aside, apply for more than one programme if you are unsure â€” you may get several Offers of Place and still only one scholarship, but you improve your chance of holding an eligible place.
If you start in July you get half now and half next February. That is a cash-flow fact worth planning around.
Watch your enrolment date. If you cannot start by the enrolment date in your Offer of Place, the scholarship is void. If your date moves, you are reassessed rather than automatically kept.
Changing your residency status mid-study can cost you the money. The University may suspend or terminate and require repayment in part or full.
Leaving or stopping study cancels the entitlement and can trigger repayment of what has already been paid.

If you want the bigger award, the International Academic Excellence Scholarship (~NZD $35,000, covering first-year accommodation and tuition in years 2 and 3) is competitive and you are invited to apply for it in eVision after accepting an earlier offer. official.description: The Victoria University of Wellington Postgraduate International Scholarship is a 10,000 NZD tuition credit for one year for new international students paying full international fees in a full-time master's degree or postgraduate diploma. There is no separate scholarship application; the award is assessed on the programme application, and the closing date is the same as the programme application closing date. The award carries detailed conditions about repayment on withdrawal, deferral within the same calendar year, and residency status changes.

official.description: The University of Turku charges tuition fees from all non-EU/EEA citizens and supports its merited and motivated students with two instruments. The Early Bird discount of EUR 2,000 is a fee discount for newly admitted master's students who accept the offer and pay the first-year tuition fee within 28 days of admission decisions. The University of Turku Merit Scholarship covers 50% of the tuition fee for the next study year, awarded on academic merit only against published credit and grade requirements, with a Finnish-language requirement. No scholarship is available to cover the first-year tuition fee.
purpose: The University of Turku charges tuition fees from all non EU/EEA citizens. The University of Turku also supports its merited and motivated students with scholarships.
"It is not possible to get a scholarship to cover the tuition fee for the first year, but the University offers an Early Bird discount of 2,000 â‚¬ for master's degree applicants."

"Scholarships are offered for both Bachelor's and Master's level studies, for students who are subject to tuition fees. Scholarships are based on studies completed at the University of Turku. All students who fulfill the requirements are eligible for a scholarship that covers 50% of the tuition fee for the next study year. The scholarships are awarded based on academic merits only."
"The University of Turku Merit Scholarship is awarded based on studies at the University of Turku and the programme the student has been admitted to."
sdg_requirement_details: No SDG or development-goal requirement is published. The published basis of the Merit Scholarship is academic merit alone - 'The scholarships are awarded based on academic merits only' - and the published targeting is financial rather than developmental: the University 'charges tuition fees from all non EU/EEA citizens' and supports 'its merited and motivated students with scholarships'.

The Early Bird discount is available only to master's degree applicants

official.degree_award: Full Bachelor's or Master's degree at the University of Turku. Both instruments are tuition-fee reductions attached to enrolment in a tuition-charging degree programme.
official.duration: Annual. The Merit Scholarship is awarded for the following academic year and is applied year by year: for master's students it covers 50% of the second-year tuition fee, and for bachelor's students it covers 50% of the second- and third-year tuition fees. It never applies to the first study year.
official.application_cycle: Annual, tied to admission. The page's information applies to students admitted in 2026; students admitted in 2025 or before are directed to a separate earlier page. The Merit Scholarship has a separate application round that opens in spring, for which the University's admission services invite all eligible applicants.
official.deadline_central_display: Two different deadlines apply to the two instruments. Early Bird discount: the applicant must accept the study offer and pay the tuition fee within 28 days after the admission decisions have been published; to receive the discount in 2026 the final date to accept the study offer and pay the tuition fee was 24 April. Merit Scholarship: "There is a separate application process for the merit scholarships. The admission services of the University will invite all eligible applicants to apply for the scholarship when the application round opens in spring." No calendar date is published for the Merit Scholarship round.
official.deadline_institutional: Two published dates, neither of them a Merit Scholarship deadline. The Merit Scholarship round is described only as opening 'in spring', with the University's admission services inviting all eligible applicants, so the operative dates sit in that invitation. The Early Bird discount has a hard published date: the applicant must accept the study offer and pay the tuition fee within 28 days after the admission decisions are published, and the published final date for 2026 was 24 April.
official.funding_label: University of Turku Merit Scholarship â€” 50% of the tuition fee for the next study year, awarded on academic merit only. Early Bird discount â€” EUR 2,000 off the tuition fee for newly admitted master's degree applicants who accept the offer and pay within 28 days of admission decisions.
official.tuition_rule: "All students who fulfill the requirements are eligible for a scholarship that covers 50% of the tuition fee for the next study year." Specifically: for master's degree students the Merit Scholarship covers 50% of the 2nd year tuition fee; for bachelor's degree students it covers 50% of the 2nd and 3rd year tuition fees. "It is not possible to get a scholarship to cover the tuition fee for the first year." The first year tuition fee has to be paid before one can register with the University.
official.home_tuition_rule: Not published. The page addresses only the University of Turku's own tuition fees and the University's own scholarships and discount. Nothing addresses fees payable to, or by, an institution in the applicant's home country, and no rule requires an applicant to disengage from a home institution.
official.host_institution_fee: Programme-specific tuition fees are published per programme and range from € 1,500 (Master's Degree Programme in European Languages, Cultures and Societies in Contact) to € 12,000 (including Master's Degree Programmes in Biomedical Imaging, Drug Discovery and Development, Public Mental Health, Biosciences, Exact Sciences, Food Development, Information and Communication Technology, Materials Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Health Technology), with € 10,000 for a number of others. The University also publishes that exceptions to these categories may apply. Critically for cash flow, 'The first year tuition fee has to be paid before one can register with the University', so the entire first-year fee is payable before any scholarship can be applied to a later year.
official.tax_status: Not published. The University of Turku states no tax treatment for the Merit Scholarship, for the 2,000 € Early Bird discount, or for the Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award.

documents: No document list is published for the Merit Scholarship on this page. What is published about the process is that there is a separate application process for merit scholarships, that the University's admission services will invite all eligible applicants to apply when the round opens in spring, and that all students who fulfil the requirements will be awarded a scholarship for the following academic year. The documents required for that round are therefore set in the spring-round invitation from the admission services, not on this page.

The documented inputs the page does give are the three published requirements against which the award is made: a credit requirement (55 credits in the first study year for a master's scholarship; 55 credits for a bachelor's 2nd-year scholarship and 110 credits across the first and second study years for a 3rd-year scholarship), a grade requirement of an average of 3.0 or higher on the 1-5 scale, and a Finnish requirement of at least 4 credits of Finnish completed before applying for the scholarship for the first time.
The Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award route is administered by the United States Fulbright program, not by the University of Turku, so its documents are outside this page.
document_format_rules: No file-size limit, accepted file type, translation rule, date-of-issue rule or signature rule is published for the Merit Scholarship or the Early Bird discount.

The binding format sources are the University's own spring-round scholarship application process - which the University says eligible applicants are invited to - and the University's separately published payment and refund policy pages for the tuition fee itself.

One published rule has a direct format consequence: 'Other previous Finnish studies or proven Finnish proficiency may also be accepted. These will be assessed on case-by-case basis.' Because the substitute evidence for the Finnish credit requirement is assessed case by case, there is no standardised form for it, and applicants relying on the substitution should expect to justify the evidence individually.

official.selection_notes: There is no competitive selection and no interview. The Merit Scholarship is deterministic: the University publishes the credit, grade and Finnish requirements, invites all eligible applicants to apply when the round opens in spring, and states that all students who fulfil the requirements will be awarded a scholarship for the following academic year. Awards are based on academic merit only, assessed from studies already completed at the University of Turku. The only discretionary element published is the Finnish-language element, where "Other previous Finnish studies or proven Finnish proficiency may also be accepted. These will be assessed on case-by-case basis." The Early Bird discount is likewise automatic for anyone meeting the 28-day condition. No assessment weighting, panel or notification date is published. One correction is published on the page and is worth noting for anyone reading older copies: "The time for accepting the study place and paying the tuition fee in order to receive the Early Bird discount was previously incorrectly stated as 30 days. The correct time is 28 days. (Information updated 10 March 2026)."

application_steps: Check whether you are charged tuition fees at all. If your first Finnish permit was for study, you still pay even after later obtaining a type A permit.

Choose a tuition-charging programme and check its published fee for 2026. Listed examples include EUR 12,000 for Master's in Biosciences, Exact Sciences, Biomedical Imaging, Drug Discovery and Development, Public Mental Health, Food Development, ICT, Materials Engineering, Mechanical Engineering and Health Technology; EUR 10,000 for Master's in Education and Learning, Human Neurosciences, East Asian Studies, Inequalities Interventions and New Welfare State, Futures Studies and Global Innovation Management, and for Bachelor's in ICT and in Sustainable and Social Entrepreneurship; and EUR 1,500 for Master's in European Languages, Cultures and Societies in Contact.
Pay the first-year tuition fee in full before you can register with the University.

If you are a master's applicant, take the Early Bird discount: accept the study offer and pay the tuition fee within 28 days after the admission decisions have been published. For 2026 the final date was 24 April.
If you are a bachelor's applicant, note that the Early Bird discount is not available to you.
Study and pay for your first study year. This is what makes you eligible for the Merit Scholarship.
In the spring, wait for the University's admission services to invite you to apply, then submit the Merit Scholarship application through the separate scholarship process.
Check you have met the credit threshold: 55 credits in the first study year (master's, or bachelor's year 2), or 110 credits across the first and second study years (bachelor's year 3).
Check your average score is at least 3.0 on the 1â€“5 grading scale.

If this is your first Merit Scholarship application, complete at least 4 Finnish credits before applying â€” these may be part of the 55-credit requirement â€” or hold other previous Finnish studies or proven Finnish proficiency for case-by-case assessment.
Receive the award. The University states all students who fulfil the requirements will be awarded a scholarship for the following academic year, worth 50% of the tuition fee.
For Bachelor's students, repeat the cycle for the third-year scholarship using the 110-credit threshold.

arrival_rules: No arrival rule, arrival deadline, visa support, relocation support or settling-in support is published for the Merit Scholarship or the Early Bird discount. Neither arrangement is cash-based, so no arrival cost component is identified.

The published timing anchor is the residence permit rule rather than an arrival date: a fixed-term continuous residence permit (A) must be valid at the beginning of each academic year, 1 August, and be granted for reasons other than studies, to exempt a student from tuition fees. That is a fee-status test, not an arrival condition.

Note the fee exemption categories are assessed in Finland - an EU Blue Card, Finnish permanent residence permit, EU Family Member's Residence Card, temporary protection status and similar - which in practice means the applicant must already hold Finnish immigration status before the fees are removed. That is an implication of the published exemption list rather than a published arrival rule, and it is recorded as such.

official.tuition_coverage: Partial, and never for the first year. The Merit Scholarship covers 50% of the tuition fee for the following academic year: 50% of the 2nd year fee for master's students, and 50% of the 2nd and 3rd year fees for bachelor's students. The first year is never covered by scholarship - the published statement is that 'It is not possible to get a scholarship to cover the tuition fee for the first year' - and the first year fee must be paid before you can register. The Early Bird discount of 2,000 € is a separate fee reduction for newly admitted master's students who accept and pay within 28 days, not a scholarship. The single exception is the Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award, which includes a scholarship covering the tuition fee, and is open only to U.S. citizens.
official.living_cost_coverage: No. Both the Merit Scholarship and the Early Bird discount are entirely about tuition fees, and neither has a published living-cost, stipend, accommodation or travel component. The published costs that remain with the student are the mandatory Student Union membership fee of around EUR 55 per academic year for bachelor's and master's students, the compulsory Student Health Care fee paid directly to Kela, and CampusSport access at EUR 78 per academic year. The Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award is the only arrangement with a published cash element, a grant of 1,000 € per month, and it is restricted to U.S. citizens.
official.international_eligibility: The whole arrangement serves students who are charged tuition. Fees are charged from citizens of countries outside the EU and EEA, or Switzerland; fees do not apply to exchange students regardless of citizenship, nor to doctoral programmes; and students in a degree programme taught in Finnish are never charged. No fees are charged from individuals who, in Finland, hold an EU Blue Card, a permanent residence permit, a continuous residence permit for purposes other than studies, a long-term resident's EU residence permit issued to third-country nationals, an EU Family Member's Residence Card, or temporary protection status. Three published caveats catch applicants out: if your first residence permit in Finland was granted for the purpose of studying you are charged even if you later obtained a continuous residence permit (type A) on other grounds; a family-tie type A permit does not exempt you if your family member originally came to Finland on a study permit; and the fixed-term continuous residence permit (A) must be valid at the beginning of each academic year, 1 August, and must be granted for reasons other than studies. The Merit Scholarship is a second-year-onward award, available to students who have paid for their studies during their first year or years. The Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award is restricted to U.S. citizens accepted to one of the University's programmes.

important_advice_for_students: Nobody gets help with year one. The University states plainly that it is not possible to get a scholarship to cover the first-year tuition fee, and that the first-year fee must be paid before you can even register. Fund that yourself.

The Early Bird discount is the single most valuable and easiest award here: EUR 2,000 off for master's applicants who accept and pay within 28 days of admission decisions. There is nothing to apply for. If you miss 28 days you lose it.

Note the correction on the University's own page: the window was previously published as 30 days and the correct figure is 28 days. If you are reading an older PDF or cached page saying 30 days, it is wrong.

The Merit Scholarship is not competitive. The University says all students who fulfil the requirements will be awarded a scholarship. Your job is simply to hit 55 credits, an average of 3.0 or better, and your Finnish requirement.

The Finnish requirement catches people out. Before your first Merit Scholarship application you need at least 4 credits of Finnish. It can count inside the 55 credits, so plan it into your first year rather than cramming it afterwards.

If you are a Bachelor's student you can hold the scholarship twice â€” 50% of year 2 and 50% of year 3. The year 3 award needs 110 credits across your first two years, so do not slack off after winning year 2.

Do not expect the scholarship to cover your living costs. Both instruments are tuition-fee reductions only. On top of tuition you still face the mandatory Student Union fee of about EUR 55 a year, the compulsory Student Health Care fee paid to Kela, CampusSport at EUR 78 a year, plus housing and food.

Check your fee exemption status before assuming you pay anything. EU/EEA and Swiss citizens, and holders of a Finnish Blue Card, permanent residence permit, non-study continuous residence permit, long-term resident's EU permit, EU Family Member's Residence Card or temporary protection status, pay no tuition at all â€” and neither of these scholarships applies to them.

Watch the residence-permit trap. If your first Finnish permit was for study, you still pay tuition even if you later obtain a type A continuous residence permit on other grounds, and the same applies to family members arriving on a studying permit.
The Early Bird discount is unavailable at Bachelor's level. Do not build a plan around it if you are applying to an undergraduate programme.

Tuition fees vary enormously by programme in 2026 â€” from EUR 1,500 for Master's in European Languages to EUR 12,000 for several science and health programmes. A 50% scholarship is worth EUR 750 in one and EUR 6,000 in another. Check your programme's published fee first.
Use the services you are paying for. Your fee funds courses outside your programme where your degree structure allows, language courses, a large research library, 24/7 IT rooms, and CampusSport.

Evidence you will need in practice, from the published requirements: confirmation that you have paid for the first study year of study at the University of Turku; your credit record showing 55 credits (or 110 credits for bachelor's year 3); your grade average showing 3.0 or higher on the 1â€“5 scale; and evidence of at least 4 credits of Finnish, or other previous Finnish studies or proven Finnish proficiency for case-by-case assessment.
For the Early Bird discount the only required action is accepting the study offer and paying the tuition fee within 28 days â€” no document is submitted to a scholarship office.

Residence-permit evidence matters for fee liability: the University publishes that a type A fixed-term continuous residence permit must be valid at the beginning of each academic year (1 August) and granted for other reasons than study in order to exempt you from fees, and that a first studying-purpose permit does not exempt you even if a later permit is obtained.

referee_tracking.instructions: The University of Turku publishes no referee, reference or recommendation requirement for the Merit Scholarship or the Early Bird discount. The Merit Scholarship is awarded on published, checkable academic criteria - credits completed, grade average, and Finnish credits - after a separate spring application that the admission services invite eligible students to. Nothing published suggests a referee is involved, so do not commission letters on the assumption that they are needed. If the spring-round invitation itself asks for something further, that invitation is the authority.

application_readiness_checklist: Confirm you are actually charged tuition. If you are an exchange student, in a doctoral programme, in a degree programme taught in Finnish, or you hold one of the published Finnish fee-exempt statuses, none of this applies to you.

Check the residence permit test carefully rather than assuming. A continuous residence permit (type A) only exempts you if it is valid at the start of each academic year on 1 August and was granted for reasons other than studies; a type A based on family ties does not exempt you if your family member came on a study permit.
Budget the first year in full. The first year fee is never covered by scholarship and must be paid before you can register - and it is the largest single cheque you will write.
Work out your programme's exact fee from the published list. They range from € 1,500 to € 12,000, so 50% is very different amounts for different programmes.

Aim for 55 ECTS in your first study year. That is the published requirement for both a master's 2nd-year scholarship and a bachelor's 2nd-year scholarship; the 3rd-year bachelor's scholarship needs 110 ECTS across the first two years.
Hold a 3.0 or higher average on the 1-5 scale. That is the published grade requirement and it is not a rounding matter.

Complete at least 4 ECTS of Finnish before you first apply. These credits can count towards the 55-credit requirement, and other Finnish studies or proven proficiency may be accepted - but only case by case.
Watch the spring invitation rather than the website. There is no published application date; the admission services invite eligible applicants when the round opens in spring.

If you are a master's applicant, the Early Bird discount is worth 2,000 € and turns on speed: accept the offer and pay within 28 days of the admission decision. The published final date for 2026 was 24 April, and the University has corrected an earlier 30-day statement to 28 days.

Do not model the Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award into your plan unless you are a U.S. citizen - it is the only arrangement here that combines a cash grant of 1,000 € per month with a full tuition scholarship, and it is nationality-restricted.

unverified_or_removed_claims: No scholarship amount was invented. The Merit Scholarship is a 50% proportion of a programme-specific fee, so choosing any euro figure as 'the amount' would have misstated the award. The published euro amounts on the page - the € 1,500 to € 12,000 fee range, the 2,000 € Early Bird discount and the 1,000 € per month Fulbright grant - are recorded in their own categories.

No living-cost, accommodation, stipend, airfare or relocation funding was recorded, because none is published. The Student Union fee, the Kela health care fee and the CampusSport price are recorded as student costs, not as scholarship items.

The Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award was not merged into the Merit Scholarship. It is a separate award with a separate grant amount and a U.S.-citizenship restriction, and it is administered through the Fulbright programme rather than by the University.

No arrival, visa or residence-permit rule was invented. The 1 August permit-validity test is recorded as a published fee-status rule, and the practical implication for immigration status is labelled as an implication rather than a published rule.

renewable was left null rather than being inferred. The Merit Scholarship is structurally renewable in the sense that it can be awarded for consecutive years as credits accumulate, but the University publishes no renewal term, so no value was asserted. The existing record's value for this field was preserved untouched.
verification.source_conflict_rule: The University of Turku's 'Tuition fees and scholarships' page and its programme pages are both University sources, and the page is the operative source for the fee, exemption, scholarship, credit, grade, Finnish and discount rules. Where the general page and the programme listing could differ on a fee, the programme-specific figure is used and the University is quoted for the possibility of exceptions. The Fulbright-University of Turku Graduate Award is named by the University but administered by the United States Fulbright program, so the University is the source of the amount and the Fulbright route governs the application; that boundary is stated rather than blurred. No third-party education site, aggregator or search result was used.
verification.source_freshness_rule: The page carries a dated correction (10 March 2026) and a 2026 Early Bird final date (24 April), and states explicitly that it carries information for students admitted in 2026, directing earlier admittees to a different page. That makes the page cycle-specific by its own wording: the fee amounts, the 28-day window, the credit and grade thresholds and the Finnish requirement must be re-read each admission cycle and must not be carried from 2026 into 2027.

purpose: NTNU's PhD (doctoral) education admits candidates to PhD programmes only where financing is secured: 'Financing is an absolute requirement for acceptance to a PhD-programme at NTNU' (published).

The published rationale for the employment model is the Norwegian system itself: 'Unlike in most other countries, PhD candidates in Norway are not considered students and PhD candidates are usually employees of the institution from which they receive their funding' (published).

The published purpose of the process is to place a doctoral candidate under supervision with a funded project: applicants are told to get in touch with a research group and secure a potential supervisor as early as possible, with at least two academic supervisors and at least one of them, usually the main supervisor, employed at NTNU (published).
sdg_requirement_details: No SDG or development-goal requirement is published. Admission is founded on a funding plan, a qualifying master's degree with a B-equivalent weighted average, a strong academic record, a project description and supervision - none of which is a development-goal criterion.

official.selection_notes: There is no competitive scholarship round. Selection is a supervisory and academic judgement made case by case, continuously through the year: the published criteria are a B-equivalent academic record, a funding plan for the whole period, a project description with its legal and ethical issues detailed, and a supervisory team in which at least one supervisor is an NTNU employee. NTNU publishes no assessment weighting, no interview requirement, no pass mark and no appeals process, and does not publish a list of the number of positions. The decisive practical point is that a strong application is a joint product - the application is 'written up in cooperation with your main supervisor', so the supervisor is a gatekeeper before any assessment happens.
application_steps: 1. Identify an available position. Positions are announced at NTNU's web pages and through jobbnorge, and admission is continuous rather than term-based.

2. Secure your funding before applying. Financing is an absolute requirement, and you must be able to document funding for the entire PhD period. Accepted routes: an NTNU or university college research fellow post, agreement with your regular employer, the Research Council of Norway's Industrial PhD or Public Sector PhD scheme, or another national or international scholarship.
3. Contact the research group and secure a potential main supervisor as early as possible - NTNU states the main supervisor should be ready when you apply.
4. Confirm you have at least two academic supervisors, with at least one (usually the main supervisor) employed at NTNU.
5. Check the individual faculty or programme for its own application form or procedures and any further qualification requirements, since these vary and can add to the central rules.
6. Complete the fixed application form.

7. Attach documentation of your former education qualifying you for a PhD, including any diploma supplement and, if available, the NOKUT assessment; and documentation of education obtained outside Norway.
8. Attach documentation of funding for the entire PhD period.

9. Write the project description, complete or preliminary. If a preliminary description is accepted, a complete version must be available within six months of admission. Detail any legal or ethical issues, and enclose ethical committee or other approvals where the project depends on them.
10. Send the application to the faculty through the department.

official.application_portal: No central application portal is published. Positions are announced at NTNU's web pages and through jobbnorge (Norway's national job market), and the application itself is sent to the faculty through the department using the fixed application form. jobbnorge is the published discovery route for salaried PhD positions; it is not an admissions system for the PhD programme, and NTNU publishes no online submission system for the programme application.
arrival_rules: No arrival rule, arrival deadline, visa support, relocation support or settling-in support is published on the pages read.

The published position on the employment relationship is that the candidate is an employee of the funding institution rather than a student, which means the practical entry formalities are employment formalities rather than student-visa formalities, but NTNU publishes no visa, residence-permission or work-permit information on this page.

Because admission is continuous rather than term-based, there is no single published start date and therefore no published arrival date. The start date is set by the individual position and the funding body.

NTNU International Researcher Support (NIRS) is published as the contact point for administrative staff and researchers working at or visiting NTNU, and as a source for people considering NTNU as a workplace and for what to expect when moving to Norway. That is information and counselling, not a published benefit of the position.

important_advice_for_students: This is a job, not a scholarship. You are applying for salaried employment, and the practical consequences - tax, pension, employment rights, notice, visa category - differ from student funding. Do not plan your finances on the assumption of a grant.

The funding plan is the first gate, not the last. NTNU states financing is an absolute requirement for acceptance, and you must be able to document funding for the entire PhD period before you are a serious candidate.

Get the supervisor first. The application is written in cooperation with your main supervisor, and at least one supervisor - usually the main one - must be an NTNU employee. That is a real precondition, not a formality.
Two supervisors, minimum. NTNU requires at least two academic supervisors, and the main supervisor must be ready at the time you apply.

Admission is continuous. There is no annual round and no central deadline, so a strong project with the right supervisor can start whenever the funding and the project align. That cuts both ways: there is also no guarantee that any particular call will happen this year.

Non-Norwegian degrees need recognition. Get a NOKUT assessment if you can, or be ready for the faculty to run its own assessment - and note that a faculty or programme may add further qualification requirements on top of the central rules.
Budget the project, not just your salary. Ethical approvals, equipment, fieldwork and travel costs are not published as covered items, so ask the department what the position budget carries.

official.description: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are prestigious international master's programmes jointly designed and delivered by at least three higher education institutions in at least three countries, with additional academic and non-academic partners. Students apply directly to the institution running the programme, and the best-ranked applicants worldwide can receive full scholarships that cover participation costs and contribute to travel, visa and a living allowance. Degrees run 1-2 academic years (60, 90 or 120 ECTS) and yield either a joint degree or at least two national degrees.
official.program_type: EU joint degree scholarship programme - Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM), a European Commission Erasmus+ action run by the Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture, in which a consortium of at least three higher education institutions in at least three countries jointly delivers a prestigious international master's, optionally with a full scholarship for its best-ranked students

The published student offer is explicit about access and merit: 'Apply for an Erasmus Mundus Joint Master. Students from all over the world are welcome. You will study at several universities in Europe and beyond. Full scholarships are available for the best students' (published).

sdg_requirement_details: No SDG or development-goal requirement is published for Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters. official.degree_award: Either a joint degree - one single degree certificate issued on behalf of at least two higher education institutions - or multiple degrees, meaning at least two degree certificates issued by two higher education institutions of the consortium. official.tuition_rule: The scholarship is the funding mechanism rather than a fee remission, and it is not automatic. The published position is that 'Masters may also offer full scholarships to the best-ranked students worldwide' - note the two operative words, 'may' and 'offer' - and that each master's website publishes 'all the steps of the application process (with and without scholarship)'. So a student on a self-funded place pays the consortium's fees, and a scholarship place is won on ranking. No fee amount, no fee-waiver mechanism and no published rule on fees at a Polish institution or at any other consortium member is published on this page.
official.home_tuition_rule: Not published. The scheme concerns fees at the participating European institutions. Nothing addresses fees payable to, or by, an institution in the applicant's home country, and no published rule requires an applicant to disengage from, or pay fees at, a home institution.
official.host_institution_fee: No host fee is published. The published institutional side of the scheme is separate and is for institutions, not students: 'Erasmus+ also offers grants to higher education institutions to run EMJM programmes', and the application route for that grant is published separately. No fee payable to a Polish or other consortium institution is described.
official.tax_status: Not published. The page states that scholarships 'contribute to' travel, visa and a living allowance but gives no statement on tax treatment, and Erasmus+ publishes no tax guidance for scholarship holders on this page. Tax treatment of an Erasmus Mundus scholarship varies by country of residence and of payment and must be checked with the awarding institution and the relevant national tax authority.

document_format_rules: No file-size limit, accepted file type, translation rule, date-of-issue rule, certification rule or signature rule is published centrally by Erasmus+ for this action.
The binding format source is the specific joint master's own application process, published on that programme's website, and it can differ from one Erasmus Mundus Joint Master to another.

One published rule has a practical format consequence: a bachelor's-equivalent level of learning must be 'officially recognised, according to national legislation and practices, in the degree awarding country', so the evidence of equivalence is a formal recognition document issued in the country where the qualification was awarded, not a self-assessment.
official.selection_notes: There is no central Erasmus+ selection. Applications go to the individual joint master, and the published scheme-level facts are that each programme sets its own entry requirements and its own application process with and without a scholarship, that a new batch of programmes is selected each year, and that scholarships go to the best-ranked students worldwide. The practical consequence is that the same student faces a different competition in each programme, and 'best-ranked' is a relative statement within a programme rather than a threshold that can be checked in advance. No published appeals process, notification date or feedback mechanism exists at scheme level.
application_steps: 1. Search the Erasmus Mundus course catalogue for the programmes on offer, and identify the joint master you want.
2. Check the programme's own website for the course of study, the list of participating universities, the entry requirements, and the full application process both with and without a scholarship.
3. Confirm you meet the entry requirement: a bachelor's degree, or the last year of one graduating before the master's starts, or an officially recognised bachelor's-equivalent level of learning.
4. Assemble the documents that programme's own website requires. Erasmus+ publishes no central list.
5. Apply directly to the institution running the programme, within that programme's own window - in most cases between October and January for a course starting the following academic year.
6. If shortlisted, expect the programme's own selection, and note that scholarship places are awarded on ranking to the best-ranked students worldwide.
7. If awarded, sign the study agreement with the relevant Erasmus Mundus Joint Master at the beginning of your studies, which is where the joint or multiple degree structure is defined in detail.

Neither is an application submission system.

Because the degree is completed across several institutions, arrivals and departures are structured by the consortium's mobility pattern, which is defined in the study agreement signed at the beginning of studies. No central rule, minimum or maximum stay per country is published.
For a Polish-coordinated programme, the Polish institution is one mobility stop among at least three institutions in at least three countries, not a sole host.

important_advice_for_students: You apply to the university, not to Brussels. Erasmus+ publishes no central application; the institution running the programme runs its own process, and that is where your ranking is decided.

The scholarship is not automatic and is not the programme. Every joint master publishes a process 'with and without scholarship', so a self-funded place is a real option and a real cost. Decide which route you are applying on before you invest effort.
'Best-ranked' is relative. The same transcript wins in a weak cohort and loses in a strong one, so choose cohorts by the supervisor and project rather than by brand.

Timing is narrow: in most cases applications go in between October and January for the following academic year. Miss it and the programme is simply closed to you for that cycle, and a new batch of programmes is added each year rather than the same one re-opening.

Confirm the degree title carefully. You will get either a joint degree or multiple degrees, and the detail is fixed in the study agreement you sign at the start - ask what exactly is on the certificate before you accept.

Weigh the money honestly: the published benefits are participation costs plus contributions to travel, visa and a living allowance, with no rates published. Get the actual figures for the specific programme and the specific scholarship route from the institution.
If you rely on a bachelor's-equivalent level of learning, get it officially recognised under the legislation of the country where you earned it. Self-assessment will not satisfy the published rule.

referee_tracking.instructions: Erasmus+ publishes no central referee requirement for Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters. Any reference requirement belongs to the specific programme, whose website is the published authority for entry requirements and the application process. Approach referees only after reading that programme's own checklist, because a reference prepared for one Erasmus Mundus Joint Master will rarely fit another.

post_award_requirements: Sign the study agreement with the relevant Erasmus Mundus Joint Master at the beginning of your studies, which is where the joint or multiple degree structure is defined in detail.
Follow the programme's published pattern of study, research, traineeship, thesis preparation and defence across the consortium's institutions.
Meet the specific financial terms of your scholarship route, which the programme publishes rather than Erasmus+.

If on a scholarship, note that it is awarded on ranking and that the published scheme provides no renewal mechanism; there is no published route to extend an EMJM scholarship beyond the programme's own duration of 1 to 2 academic years.

Complete the requirements of the degree itself in at least two institutions, since the published award is either a joint degree on behalf of at least two higher education institutions or multiple degrees from at least two of them.
questions_to_ask_host: Is this programme a currently selected Erasmus Mundus Joint Master, and in which year's batch was it selected?
Which institutions are in the consortium, which countries, and where in the pattern does the Polish institution sit?
Will I receive a joint degree or multiple degrees, and exactly what appears on the certificate or certificates?
How many scholarships are available, how many applicants were there last cycle, and what does 'best-ranked' mean operationally here?
For the scholarship route, what are the actual amounts for participation costs, travel, visa and the living allowance, and are they paid in monthly instalments?
What is the exact application deadline, and is there a separate earlier deadline for scholarship consideration?
What is the exact breakdown of the published October-to-January application window, and are there interviews?
Are there language requirements, and does the programme waive or reduce tuition fees for self-funded students as well?
What happens to the scholarship if I defer, if I fail a module, or if the consortium changes my mobility country?

institution_check_required: This record is a country slice of a scheme, not a single scholarship. Every Poland-specific fact - which Polish institutions coordinate or participate, which joint masters are currently selected, the entry requirements, the application steps, the documents, the formats, the scholarship amounts, the tuition position and the deadline - is set by the individual joint master and is published on that programme's own website, not by Erasmus+. None of it is on the page read.

deadline_central deliberately null: there is no Erasmus+ central student deadline. The published pattern is October to January for entry the following academic year, and each programme sets its own dates. deadline_institutional records that.

funding_amount deliberately null: the published benefits are four qualitative categories - participation costs and contributions to travel, visa and a living allowance - with no rate published. The single categories are recorded in coverage and funding_type is Full Funding because participation costs are covered, but no figure is invented.

tax_status deliberately null: no tax treatment is published. For a multi-country mobility programme with a living allowance, this is a material gap and must be checked with the awarding institution and the relevant national tax authority.

tuition_rule records the published structure rather than a fee outcome, because the central page describes a scholarship that covers participation costs and separately publishes an application process 'with and without scholarship'. Whether a self-funded place is fee-bearing, and whether any fee is charged to a Polish institution, is programme-specific and unpublished centrally.

host_institution_fee, home_tuition_rule and arrival_rules are recorded as unpublished centrally. No host fee, no home-country fee rule, no arrival deadline, no visa support and no minimum stay per country is published on this page.

renewable recorded as false on the published scheme design: an EMJM is a 1 to 2 academic year degree with participation costs funded for that period, and no renewal or extension mechanism is published. If a specific programme publishes a repeat year, that programme governs.
deferrable, return_home_required and clinical_restriction deliberately null: no deferral mechanism, no return-home obligation and no subject or clinical restriction is published at scheme level.

documents, document_format_rules, selection_criteria and selection_notes are recorded as scheme-level statements with the programme as the authority. The published selection facts are the accreditation gate, the first-degree gate, and scholarships going to 'the best-ranked students worldwide'; no weighting, interview format, pass mark or appeals process is published centrally.

The record's own second official source, the EACEA Erasmus Mundus catalogue, was not read in this pass. It is the place to establish the current list of selected joint masters and which of them involve Polish institutions.
unverified_or_removed_claims: No scholarship amount, stipend figure, travel contribution or visa contribution figure was invented. The four published benefit categories are recorded without rates.
No Polish institution, programme name, quota or national eligibility condition was asserted. Nothing on the page read identifies Polish participation, so any such claim would have been invention.

No immigration or tax consequence was inferred from multi-country mobility. arrival_rules records only the published travel and visa contributions and the study agreement, and states the absence of a published rule.
No selection weighting or assessment method was invented; the published 'best-ranked' language is recorded as the scheme-level criterion, with selection otherwise attributed to each programme.

renewable was set false with the reasoning recorded, because a 1 to 2 academic year degree with participation costs funded and no published renewal route supports it - but it is flagged in institution_check_required rather than presented as a published rule.
verification.source_conflict_rule: The European Commission's Erasmus+ page is the scheme-level authority and is the only source read in this pass. The individual joint master's website governs its own entry requirements, application steps, documents, formats, amounts and deadline, because Erasmus+ itself states that 'Each master's website has all the details'. The Erasmus Mundus Association is a published applicant-support resource and is treated as guidance, not as an awarding authority. The EACEA catalogue, though cited on the record, is a catalogue of selected programmes and does not override either the Commission page or a programme's own site.
verification.source_freshness_rule: The page carries a 'Last updated: 26 June 2025' stamp, so all scheme-level statements are current to that date. Because a new batch of programmes is selected each year and the catalogue is refreshed annually, the set of currently selected joint masters - and any participation by Polish institutions - must be re-established from the catalogue each cycle. Programme-level money, dates and requirements change with each cohort and must be read from the programme's own page.

data_quality.coverage: High on the scheme design - consortium structure, degree types, duration, entry gate, application route, published benefit categories, application window and the fact that a new batch is selected annually. Zero on anything Poland-specific, and nothing on amounts, taxes, fees, documents, formats or programme-level deadlines, because all of those sit with the individual joint master. The EACEA catalogue, which is where the Polish institutional question would be settled, was not read.

official.description: Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters are prestigious international master's programmes jointly designed and delivered by at least three higher education institutions in at least three countries, with additional academic and non-academic partners. Students apply directly to the institution running the programme, and the best-ranked applicants worldwide can receive full scholarships that cover participation costs and contribute to travel, visa and a living allowance. Degrees run 1-2 academic years (60, 90 or 120 ECTS) and yield either a joint degree or at least two national degrees.
official.program_type: EU joint degree scholarship programme - Erasmus Mundus Joint Masters (EMJM), a European Commission Erasmus+ action run by the Directorate-General for Education, Youth, Sport and Culture, in which a consortium of at least three higher education institutions in at least three countries jointly delivers a prestigious international master's, optionally with a full scholarship for its best-ranked students
